plain: v0 is a Vercel tool where you describe a screen in words and it draws it for you, working: a homepage, a dashboard with charts, a form, a table with filters. It doesn't build the whole application with its database the way Lovable does; it builds the part you see, and does it very well. It's used two ways: to quickly get the screen for something you're going to build, or to get design ideas when you don't know where to start. What you walk away with is the code for that screen, ready to paste into your project.

account.free: Free plan with a limited number of messages per month, enough to test it out and get one or two screens. Paid plans started around $20 a month as of August 2026. As with all these tools, you spend per message, not per time: five separate fixes cost five times as much as one well-written brief. Check the current price at v0.app.
steps: It's made by Vercel, the same company behind the site-publishing tool. If you already have a Vercel account, it works with the same one.
It's the most practical option: if you later want to bring the code into your own project, everything is already connected.

The box in the center. The more specific you are about what's on screen and who it's for, the less generic the result. "A dashboard" gives you a textbook dashboard; "a dashboard for a shop owner who wants to see today's sales, with four numbers up top and an orders table below" gives you something usable.
It usually proposes more than one version. Compare them before you start fixing the first one: sometimes the second is much closer to what you wanted.
Get the code or publish it
You can copy the screen's code to paste into your project, or publish it directly to get a link to show people. To show someone quickly, publishing is fastest.
In the account settings. Knowing how many messages you have left changes how you write the next one.
account.warning: What comes out of here is the screen, not the application. The buttons can look gorgeous and do nothing, and the data you see is usually made up for the example. Don't show it to a client saying 'it's already built': show it for what it is, a design that works on screen, or you'll be committing to an impossible deadline.

first: Describe ONE screen, not an application. "The homepage", "the contact form", "the sales dashboard". One at a time.
Say who it's for and where they're coming from. That changes the design more than any adjective you could add.
Compare the variants it proposes before fixing anything.
Fix by pointing at the specific element, not by describing the whole screen again.
Publish the link and open it on your phone. That's where you see whether the design holds up.
shortcuts: Where you describe the screen. Specific wins: what's on it, who it's for, and what the person entering it needs to be able to do.
Gives you several versions of the same thing. Looking at all of them before fixing anything saves messages and sometimes gives you an idea you hadn't asked for.
You click the specific button or text in the preview and talk about that one thing. Much more precise than describing it in words.
You take the component to paste into your project. It's written in React and Tailwind, which is the standard today.
Gives you a public link instantly to show someone. It's the fast way to gather feedback.
You can give it a screenshot of a screen you like or a hand-drawn sketch, and work from there. It works surprisingly well.
Every change is saved. When a fix makes the design worse, you go back instead of trying to undo it with words.
If you already use Vercel, you can bring the screen into one of your projects without copying and pasting by hand.
daily: One screen per brief. Asking for "the whole application" produces five mediocre screens instead of one good one.
Start with mobile. Explicitly say it should be designed for narrow screens first; widening it afterward is easy, narrowing a desktop design down is a mess.
Give it a visual reference if you have one. A screenshot of a website you like saves twenty adjectives and lands much closer.

Ask for the states people forget: what it looks like while loading, what it looks like if the list is empty, and what it looks like if something fails. Almost no first version includes them, and they're half the real experience.
Be clear that the data is fake. What you see in the table is made up; connecting it to real data is a separate job and the one that takes time.
Save the code to your project as soon as possible. What only lives inside the tool ends up lost among twenty experiments.

templates.name: The screen brief that doesn't come out generic
templates.what: The gap between what v0 returns for "make me a dashboard" and what it returns for this is huge. This brief gives it the one thing it can't invent on its own: who it's for, what that person decides looking at the screen, and what they need to be able to do.
templates.how: 1) One screen per brief. 2) Be literal about the data shown: column names, the numbers up top. 3) Always keep the states section: it's what separates a showcase design from a usable one. 4) Paste it and compare the variants before fixing anything.
fill: Who's entering and from which device. Changes the entire design
What this person looks at and what they do next. It's what orders the visual hierarchy
Real column and metric names, not "data"
Loading, empty, and error. Nobody asks for them and they're all needed
templates.code:
Design ONE screen. Just one, not the whole application.

WHICH SCREEN: [e.g.: the dashboard the shop owner sees on login]

WHO FOR: [e.g.: a corner-shop owner, 50 years old, comes in
from their phone in the morning while opening up]

WHAT THEY DECIDE LOOKING AT IT: [e.g.: whether they need to
restock something today and whether there's any order left unprepared]

WHAT'S ON SCREEN, top to bottom:
1. [e.g.: four big numbers: today's sales, pending orders,
   out-of-stock products, returns]
2. [e.g.: a table with today's orders: time, customer, amount,
   status]
3. [e.g.: a big button to mark an order as prepared]

STATES I ALSO WANT TO SEE (always forgotten):
- What it looks like while data is loading.
- What it looks like if there are no orders today.
- What it looks like if the data failed to load.

HOW: design for mobile first and let it adapt to large screens.
Large, readable type. Plenty of white space. No animations.
All text in natural English.

Give me two different versions so I can compare.

errors: The screen is pretty but the buttons don't do anything

Not a bug: v0 designs the part you see, not the part that works. The data is fake and the buttons are fake. Connecting it to real data is the next job, and it's the one that takes time. Be clear about this yourself before showing it to anyone.
It comes out generic, like any template off the internet

Your brief was generic. "A modern dashboard" produces everyone's dashboard. Rewrite it saying who it's for, what that person decides looking at it, and which concrete columns and numbers appear. Concrete nouns do more than adjectives.
The code it gives me doesn't work when I paste it into my project

Almost always the pieces it depends on are missing: the component library, the styling configuration, or some dependency. Ask explicitly: "tell me everything I need to install and configure for this component to work in a freshly created Next.js project, step by step."
Plan exhausted. Take the chance to gather all your fixes into one list and send them together when it resets. You'll get further with five well-written messages than with twenty scattered ones.
You didn't ask for it in that order. Always say "design for mobile first and let it adapt to large screens." Doing it in that order works; the reverse almost always causes problems.
The text comes out in Spanish or another language
By default it generates in English. Ask explicitly: "all text in natural English, including buttons, form labels, and error messages."

prompts.name: Turn a vague idea into a screen brief
prompts.prompt: I want to design a screen with v0 and I know what I need but I can't describe it, so it comes out generic. Help me write the brief. One: ask me up to four questions about who's going to use this screen, from which device, what they decide looking at it, and what they do right after. Two: write me the final brief ready to paste, describing what's on screen top to bottom with concrete names for columns, buttons, and metrics, not vague categories. Three: always include the request for the three states everyone forgets: loading, empty list, and error. Four: tell me what I've packed into this screen that should actually be a separate screen, because cramming everything into one is the classic mistake. Five: tell me which two well-known visual references resemble what I want, so I can decide if that's the direction to go. Six: at the end, remind me that what comes out is only the design and not a working application, with a sentence I can use if I show it to a client. What I need is: [DESCRIBE IT AS BEST YOU CAN].

prompts.name: Integrate what v0 gave me into my project
prompts.prompt: I have the code for a component v0 generated and I want to plug it into my project without breaking anything. I don't code well: tell me exactly what to do. One: look at the code I'm pasting and tell me what it needs to work: which libraries to install, what configuration is needed, and whether it depends on a file I don't have. Two: give me the terminal commands one at a time, with what should show up after each one. Three: tell me which file in my project this component belongs in and how it's used from another screen. Four: the data it brings is fake: tell me exactly which lines need to change so it reads real data, and what shape that data needs to have. Five: warn me if anything in this code clashes with what I already have, especially in styles. Six: tell me how to verify it's working before I call anything done. My project is: [WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT'S BUILT WITH]. The code is: [PASTE IT].

words: Component
A reusable piece of screen: a button, a card, a table. It's the unit v0 works with.
Variant
Each of the different versions it proposes for the same brief. Compare them before fixing anything.
Mock data
The made-up data you see on screen. It's for designing; it doesn't come from anywhere real.
React
The way of building web screens that v0 uses. You don't need to know it to work here, but you do to touch the code afterward.
Tailwind
The way it styles the code it generates. You'll see odd-looking names attached to every element: those are the styles.
Responsive
The screen adapting to the phone's width. Achieved by designing for mobile first, not the other way around.
Empty state
What shows when there's nothing to display. Almost nobody asks for it, and it's half the real experience.
Publish (deploy)
Putting the screen at an internet address to show someone.
Prompt
The brief. Here what works is describing what's on screen, not what feeling you want to convey.
Vercel
The company that makes v0 and also the course's site-publishing tool. They share an account.
matters: Being clear, and saying so, that this is the design and not the application. Showing it as if it were already built is how you end up committed to an impossible deadline.
Always asking for the three states: loading, empty, and error. A design that only handles the happy path falls apart on the first day of real use.
Describing who it's for and what that person decides. It's the one thing v0 can't invent, and the one thing that keeps it from producing everyone's template.
Designing for mobile first. It works in that order; the other way around, almost never.
ignore: Fine-tuning color and spacing on early attempts. First the screen has to say what it needs to say; polish comes last and is fast.
Trying to get v0 to build the entire application with its database. Not what it's for: that's what Lovable or a real project is for.
The code, while you're still exploring ideas. Once a screen convinces you, that's when it's worth looking at and taking it with you.
